title: Read filtering happens on IReactorClient, not inside IReactor, so reactor.get() and client.get() return different documents in the same process
content:
A read produces no operation. It has no position in any stream, so admission cannot gate it, replay cannot re-evaluate it and no append condition can guard it — the positional machinery cannot see reads at all. Read enforcement therefore lives on the reactor's **own read surface**: the `IReactorClient`.

Two placement facts follow, both demonstrated by the `scoped-reads` recipe on one document in one process:

- **`IReactor` serves everything.** It is inside the trust boundary; internal consumers — the event bus, read models, processors — need unfiltered data to build their projections, and whatever they re-expose is their own read surface to gate. So `reactor.getByIdOrSlug()` hands all four scopes to anyone while `client.get()` hands Mallory only `auth` and `document`.
- **The gate carries no feature flag of its own.** A client over a reactor with `featureFlags: {}` still filters reads, so a policy is enforced against readers before it is enforced against writers. What `authEnforcement` changes is *which model* answers: with it on, the read gate builds the registered decision model at the stream heads and evaluates a `read` request per scope, so `{ group }` and conditional read grants apply; below it, a read evaluates the bare policy alone.

Every read carries a subject — the client defaults it to its own signer, a server passes the authenticated caller — and a write hands back a read: the document `client.execute()` returns is gated exactly like `get()`, as the client's own identity. A custom subgraph or server that reads through the client inherits all of this and cannot forget to enforce.

Two engineering rules the spec records: the model is built through the **read side, never the write cache** (a reactor whose executors live in worker processes holds parent state no commit invalidates, so a read there would decide against a stale policy); and a read of a document's *operations* fetches the whole document, because evaluating a condition on the gated scope's state needs more than the policy.

Timing differs from writes: an operation is evaluated at its position, so a revocation catches operations accepted before it arrived, but a read is evaluated when it is served — revoking read only stops future serving and cannot recall bytes a replica already holds.
